background: (inferred) A woman who drinks wine regularly at home to unwind, likely has a job or daily routine that leads to evening relaxation, and is currently taking medication for depression.
self_view_of_problem: She sees her drinking as a way to make things 'more interesting' when feeling down, but acknowledges she sometimes drinks more than intended and feels worse afterward.
resistance_drivers: Resists external benchmarks (like the seven-drink guideline) by setting a personal, less stringent goal ('two drinks a night').
Minimizes the severity of her drinking by contrasting it with not getting 'crazy' or out of control.
(inferred) Deflects deeper exploration of the depression-drinking link by focusing on practical steps (like having less wine in the house).

ambivalence.for_change: She is ready to cut back because she doesn't want to make her depression worse.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is emotionally attached to drinking as a tool to make life feel more interesting and less blur when she is down.

values_and_stakes: Her evening relaxation routine (watching movies, reading, taking baths) which is intertwined with drinking.
Her sense of control over her own habits and goals, rather than adhering to external medical guidelines.
(inferred) Her current coping mechanism for depression, which she risks losing if she cuts back significantly.
key_facts: She drinks at least 12 drinks a week, averaging three to four drinks per occasion.
She sometimes finishes a bottle of wine in one night, which constitutes binge drinking.
She has agreed to a goal of cutting back to two drinks per night.

background: (inferred) A man who drinks socially with friends and is being treated for ADHD.
self_view_of_problem: He does not see his drinking as a problem because he doesn't get 'fallen down drunk' or drink every night, and it's part of his social life.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by comparing his drinking to more extreme examples when challenged.
Questions or doubts factual information presented by the therapist.
Minimizes the significance of his drinking by framing it as normal and non-problematic.

ambivalence.for_change: He acknowledges that knowing about the health risks gives him something to think about.
ambivalence.against_change: He feels attached to the social enjoyment and taste of beer, and changing would threaten that routine.

values_and_stakes: His social life and friendships centered around going to bars.
The enjoyment and sensory pleasure he gets from drinking beer.
(inferred) His self-image as a healthy person who doesn't have problems.
key_facts: He drinks two to three days a week, typically five or six beers per occasion.
He only considers changing if he experiences a direct negative consequence like getting sick.
He is receiving treatment for ADHD.

background: (inferred) An adult recently diagnosed with diabetes, likely with a sedentary lifestyle and dietary habits contributing to the condition.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as needing to 'learn about my-- how to manage my diabetes' and sees it as 'massive' and 'a huge amount of stuff to do' that he's not certain he can do.
resistance_drivers: Expresses immediate doubt and uncertainty when presented with the full scope of required lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, medication).
Responds with sighs and overwhelmed withdrawal when confronted with the serious consequences of inaction.

ambivalence.for_change: He is scared by the doctor's warnings about losing eyesight and feet, which pulls him toward learning management.
ambivalence.against_change: He feels overwhelmed by the perceived enormity and difficulty of the lifestyle changes required, pulling him away from engagement.

values_and_stakes: His physical health and bodily integrity (eyesight, feet) are at immediate risk.
(inferred) His current lifestyle habits and dietary preferences, which provide comfort and routine, are at risk.
key_facts: His A1C or blood glucose is very high, indicating serious, uncontrolled diabetes.
He was recently diagnosed, so the condition and required management are new to him.
The doctor 'really laid into' him about the seriousness, which scared him.

background: A person with a felony conviction (non-violent, drug possession) who has gone back to school and earned a degree, is seeking professional or corporate-level work, and is currently starting a small event planning business. (inferred) He is Middle Eastern and has a brother who has tried to help him find work.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as his criminal history being an overwhelming, permanent barrier that blocks him from becoming a 'good productive member of society' and causes him to consider 'going back to what I know', leading to resurging anger and depression.
resistance_drivers: Deflects or expresses uncertainty ('I don't know') when asked to analyze the problem or consider new actions.
Rejects potential solutions by highlighting why they won't work (e.g., advocacy groups offer only dead-end jobs, disclosing early leads to immediate rejection for good jobs).
Minimizes his own agency and externalizes blame, framing societal and systemic forces as insurmountable.

ambivalence.for_change: He explicitly states a desire to be productive, stay on the right path, and not fall back into a destructive lifestyle of crime or substance use.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to a self-concept as a wronged victim of an unfair system, which provides a justification for his frustration and shields him from the full risk of trying and failing on his own merits.

values_and_stakes: His identity as a 'good productive member of society' and a professional, which is threatened by accepting low-wage or 'dead-end' jobs.
The hope and self-worth derived from his educational achievement and qualifications, which are jeopardized by continued rejection.
His current stability and mental health, which he fears will collapse into 'destructive behavior' if he becomes too discouraged.
key_facts: He has a Class 1 felony conviction that requires a governor's pardon for expungement, a process he finds daunting.
He recently had a promising job interview arranged by his brother that fell through when he disclosed his record during the background check.
He has started his own event planning business as an alternative path to income and self-employment.

background: (inferred) A divorced woman who recently moved to Portland, likely middle-aged given the health context and mention of a son.
self_view_of_problem: She initially frames her drinking as not a significant problem, stating 'I don't think it's that much of a problem' and 'not really' a problem, but after learning it's linked to her blood pressure, she concedes 'that could be a problem'.
resistance_drivers: Expresses disbelief and minimizes when presented with medical guidelines (e.g., 'Are you serious?', 'Seven drinks in a week doesn't seem like that much?').

Attributes increased drinking to external life changes (divorce, move) to deflect from the severity ('I know my drinking has increased a little since I got divorced and moved to Portland, but I don't think it's that much of a problem').

ambivalence.for_change: She acknowledges that drinking might be affecting her blood pressure and recalls a fall that drinking 'probably didn't help', and her son expresses concern, which she finds 'scary'.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is attached to drinking as a social routine and coping mechanism post-divorce, and reducing it feels like a loss of comfort and autonomy.

values_and_stakes: Her health, specifically managing her blood pressure to avoid future medical problems.
Her relationship with her son, who 'keeps telling me that I'm drinking too much'.
(inferred) Her social connection and routine at the local pub, which she frequents four times a week.
key_facts: She drinks wine at a pub down the street about four times a week, consuming three to six glasses per occasion.
She fell earlier in the year walking home from the bar and hurt her shoulder.
She rates her readiness to cut back as a 6 on a 0-10 scale.

background: (inferred) A person with a busy schedule who has a gym membership and has been thinking about working out.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is a lack of time and motivation to fit working out into a busy schedule.
resistance_drivers: Deflects direct criticism by reframing the problem as logistical (e.g., responds to being called 'lazy' by citing a busy schedule).
Resists therapist's specific prescriptions by amplifying practical obstacles (e.g., counters the suggested workout frequency/duration by detailing commute time).

ambivalence.for_change: She wants to start working out again and believes she needs to do it.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is attached to her current schedule and the identity of being a busy, non-lazy person, making change feel like an overwhelming imposition.

values_and_stakes: Her current schedule and time allocation.
Her self-view as a competent, busy person rather than a lazy one.
key_facts: She has a gym membership.
She believes a realistic workout session takes two hours, not one.
The therapist directly challenged her to report going to the gym by their next session.

background: (inferred) A woman who is socially isolated and seeking to build connections, likely not currently employed outside the home.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as needing to go out and join activities to make friends, but is held back by the fear that no one will like her and she won't have friends there.
resistance_drivers: Expresses passive agreement ('Yes, I guess') when the therapist introduces a task she hasn't completed, signaling initial reluctance to engage with the topic.
Immediately follows a statement of non-action with a detailed plan of potential activities, deflecting from her failure to act by focusing on future possibilities.

ambivalence.for_change: She states she is going to do it anyway because 'this is what I need to do to make friends', acknowledging the action is necessary for her desired change.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is emotionally attached to avoiding the intense anxiety and potential social rejection she anticipates from joining a group.

values_and_stakes: The potential for forming new friendships and social connections.
(inferred) Her sense of self-worth and identity as a likable person, which is threatened by the fear of rejection.
(inferred) Her current state of safety and emotional equilibrium, which would be disrupted by venturing into unfamiliar social settings.
key_facts: She identified specific, affordable activities (YMCA classes, a $10 yoga class at the Women's Center) she considered attending.
She explicitly did not attend any of the activities she had considered.
She directly voiced her core fear: 'what if no-one likes me? What if I don't have friends in there?'

background: (inferred) A teenager or young adult who attends parties and has a sexual partner, likely in a school or social environment where peer drinking is common.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as 'drinking too much' at parties, which leads to forgetting things and risking STDs, but does not see themselves as needing help or having an alcohol use disorder.
resistance_drivers: Rejects diagnostic labels when therapist suggests alcohol use disorder, asserting independence ('that's not me, I don't need help from anyone').
Minimizes drinking frequency and context ('really only drink at parties', 'somewhere around eight days, I'm not sure') when asked about quantity.
(inferred) Deflects personal responsibility by attributing condom non-use to mutual intoxication ('we just didn't stop', 'we weren't thinking that way').

ambivalence.for_change: I really don't want any STDs and I don't like wondering whether I have one or not.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I enjoy the social fun and relaxation drinking provides with friends, and changing might mean losing that ease and connection.

values_and_stakes: Social belonging and fun at parties with friends who drink.
Autonomy and self-reliance (not needing help from anyone).
Sexual health and avoiding STDs with a specific partner.
key_facts: The client drinks four or five drinks at parties, which they consider 'too much'.
The client had unprotected sex while drinking with a partner they have had sex with before.
The client has a friend who thinks they drink too much and could help them limit drinks.

background: (inferred) An older adult who is trying to incorporate regular gym visits into their life, likely with a busy schedule and a history of inactivity.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as needing to build up consistency with exercise and diet, seeing it as 'still hard' and requiring patience, while being easily sidetracked by a hectic schedule and discouraged by comparing themselves to younger gym-goers.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from deeper commitment by focusing on external comparisons (e.g., younger 'buff' guys) that make the goal feel discouragingly distant.
Minimizes progress or sets conditions for future change (e.g., needing to see more gym results before fully committing to dietary changes).
(inferred) Uses a busy schedule as a rationale for inconsistency, framing lapses as external rather than internal motivational issues.

ambivalence.for_change: He feels better physically (back hurts less, pants fit better) and is pleased with the progress, which pulls him toward continuing.
ambivalence.against_change: He is attached to the immediate gratification of old habits (like junk food) and feels an internal pull toward the identity of his 'normal rational self' who sees ambitious fitness goals as age-inappropriate and too much work.

values_and_stakes: Physical comfort and reduced pain (his back hurting less and pants fitting better).
A sense of rational self-control and age-appropriate identity (not wanting to chase being 'buff').
(inferred) The pleasure and convenience of his current dietary habits and schedule flexibility.
key_facts: He went to the gym twice in the recent period (once on Thursday and again on Saturday).
He did not go to the gym at all until Thursday last week, indicating a pattern of procrastination or scheduling difficulty.
He has started having 'second thoughts' before eating junk food, showing a nascent cognitive shift regarding diet.

background: A parent of a young child named Aiden who has had multiple ear infections. (inferred) Likely a primary caregiver managing work and childcare.
self_view_of_problem: Frames the problem as the stress of Aiden's ear infections and the difficulty of quitting smoking, saying 'It's just really-- It's really, really hard.'
resistance_drivers: Deflects by emphasizing effort and mitigation ('I try really hard not to smoke around him') when confronted about the link between smoking and harm.
Uses 'I don't know' and passive agreement ('Okay, whatever') to shut down direct pressure and demands for commitment.
Dismisses concrete solutions by citing practical barriers ('I just don't have time for any of that').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) Wants to reduce Aiden's suffering and stress from the ear infections.
ambivalence.against_change: Feels overwhelmed by the perceived difficulty of quitting and attached to smoking as a coping mechanism.

values_and_stakes: Aiden's health and well-being, specifically avoiding further ear infections and medical procedures.
(inferred) Her self-image as a caring, responsible parent who tries hard.
(inferred) Her personal time and routine, which would be disrupted by quitting methods.
key_facts: Her child Aiden has had six or seven ear infections in the past year.
She smokes but does not smoke in the car or inside the home when Aiden is there.
She has previously thought about quitting but has not taken action.

background: (inferred) A person in therapy for self-harm and suicidal ideation, likely with a history of repeated self-injury and prior emergency room visits.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is that their life is not going better and the therapist is not helping them or being available when they need help.
resistance_drivers: Deflects with sarcasm or rhetorical questions when asked for factual details about self-harm (e.g., 'Um, pretty obvious [chuckles]', 'What do you mean what I did?').
Expresses direct blame and anger toward the therapist when discussing the cause of self-harm, framing the therapist's unavailability as the trigger.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They want their life to go better and seek help, as evidenced by calling the therapist.
ambivalence.against_change: They are attached to a narrative where the therapist's failure justifies their self-harm, making change feel like surrendering a justified grievance.

values_and_stakes: The therapeutic relationship itself, as they explicitly stake their safety and improvement on the therapist's availability and effectiveness.
(inferred) A sense of control or self-agency, as their self-harm is presented as a logical consequence ('might as well just go all the way') when help fails.
key_facts: The client cut themselves deeply with a razor on their arm, in a pattern they describe as 'same as always'.
The client directly links the deep cutting to calling the therapist for help and not receiving it.
The client has not sought medical care (like ER stitches) for these deep cuts, citing a negative prior experience.

background: She is a single mother with a two-year-old son, works full-time as a server at a restaurant, and is attending night classes for culinary arts.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as childcare being her biggest issue, specifically her mother's unreliability causing her to miss work and class.
resistance_drivers: Deflects with financial constraints when therapist suggests paid childcare options.
Expresses generalized distrust of others when asked about alternative caregivers beyond her mother.

ambivalence.for_change: She acknowledges that reliable childcare would reduce her stress and help her meet her work and school commitments.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She feels a protective attachment to being the sole judge of who is trustworthy with her son, which makes exploring new arrangements emotionally risky.

values_and_stakes: Her son's safety and well-being, which she feels only she can adequately ensure.
Her progress in culinary school and her job, which depend on reliable childcare.
(inferred) Her relationship with her mother, whose support, however unreliable, is a valued connection.
key_facts: Her mother has backed out of childcare at the last minute multiple times, causing her to miss work and class.
A neighbor with a three-year-old daughter successfully watched her son once in an emergency.
Her son will turn three in a couple of months, making him eligible for programs like Head Start.

background: (inferred) The client is an employed adult with a social life that includes going out to bars with friends and taking trips to Las Vegas, and they have friends at work who smoke.
self_view_of_problem: The client does not view themselves as a smoker or tobacco user, framing their use of cigarillos as a purely social, occasional, and harmless activity that is distinct from a 'real' smoking habit.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes and redefines behavior when confronted with evidence of harm (e.g., insists it's not cigarettes, not a habit, and not daily use).
Resists the 'smoker' label and its associated identity threat, even after acknowledging physical damage and daily use.
(inferred) Deflects by comparing their behavior to a more severe stereotype (e.g., 'not a chain smoker') when the therapist highlights the scope of the behavior.

ambivalence.for_change: They are concerned about developing serious health issues like cancer and want to reverse the oral damage they've already sustained.
ambivalence.against_change: They are emotionally attached to the social identity, relaxation, and sense of sophistication that smoking cigarillos with friends provides.

values_and_stakes: Their social connections and shared rituals with friends during nights out and work breaks.
The enjoyable and sophisticated experiences associated with activities like visiting cigar bars in Las Vegas.
(inferred) Their self-concept as a person who made a conscious decision to avoid cigarettes and is not a 'smoker'.
key_facts: The client has developed nicotinic stomatitis, a physical condition caused by tobacco use.
The client smokes Swisher Sweets cigarillos, including one or two daily during work breaks and when socializing.
The client rated their confidence in quitting as a seven or eight on a ten-point scale.

background: (inferred) A person in California who has been mandated or referred to therapy after being found with a small amount of marijuana, likely due to a legal or institutional requirement.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a procedural hurdle to 'get behind' them, minimizing the significance of the marijuana ('a little bag', 'not a lot', 'no one cares').
resistance_drivers: Minimizes the severity of the issue when it is introduced ('It's not a lot though', 'It's not like I was gonna sell it').
Expresses impatience and a desire to expedite the process when the therapist's role is implied ('How long is this gonna take?', 'I just wanna get whatever I need to get done, done').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to complete the mandated requirements to avoid further negative consequences.
ambivalence.against_change: An attachment to the view that the behavior is socially acceptable and not a real problem ('It's California, no one cares').

values_and_stakes: (inferred) Personal autonomy and freedom from mandated oversight or control.
(inferred) Time and efficiency, not wanting this process to be a prolonged burden.
key_facts: A small bag of marijuana was found in the client's possession.
The client is in a setting (likely California) where they perceive marijuana use as socially inconsequential.
The therapeutic contact is structured over six months with sessions of limited duration (15-20 minutes).

background: She is an aspiring social worker, a mother, and was engaged to a long-distance truck driver but has called off the engagement.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as a 'battle between mind and heart' where her heart wants a true family unit with togetherness for her son, but her mind says the relationship is not going that way and she can't change her partner.
resistance_drivers: Resists accepting the status quo when it conflicts with her ideal of family togetherness, stating she doesn't want to 'subject to just accepting things the way they are'.
Expresses frustration and confusion about having to repeatedly explain her needs, indicating resistance to prolonged emotional processing or 'going over the problem over and over'.
(inferred) Shows reluctance to fully explore her own emotional needs and vulnerability, as she identifies as the 'receiver' and caretaker for others but struggles to open up herself.

ambivalence.for_change: She wants to 'stabilize myself to be the best parent that I can be' and avoid hurting herself in the long run by accepting a relationship that doesn't meet her needs.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is emotionally attached to the ideal of a collaborative, together family unit and fears losing that dream, which represents her core vision of providing 'more than what I had' for her son.

values_and_stakes: Her son's upbringing and the 'great environment' she wants to provide for him.
The ideal of family 'togetherness' and a collaborative parental team, modeled after her own parents' civility.
Her identity as a proactive problem-solver and 'collaborating person' in relationships.
key_facts: Her fiancé is a long-distance truck driver who is gone for days, up to a week at a time.
She called off her engagement with her son's father because they were 'not at that connection anymore'.
She realized yesterday she had no one to talk to because she is always the listener for others.

background: Katie is a college student on an academic scholarship, the first in her family to attend college, and she is on the debate team.
self_view_of_problem: She frames her marijuana use as 'not a big deal' and 'just like a couple times a week to relax' to manage anxiety and fit in with peers, but acknowledges it 'doesn't sound like a very good habit' when the downsides are summarized.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by minimizing the problem when her behavior is questioned (e.g., citing decriminalization, calling it 'not a big deal').
Expresses hesitation and uncertainty when asked to consider change or new solutions (e.g., 'I don't know', 'I'm not sure it is').
Resists based on family norms and financial constraints when counseling is suggested (e.g., 'We don't do that kind of thing in my family', 'I don't have the money for it').

ambivalence.for_change: She admits the habit isn't good and feels stress from hiding it, worrying about getting caught, and feeling embarrassed about bumming it.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is emotionally attached to marijuana as a tool for relaxation and social belonging, fearing that without it she might not cope with anxiety or fit in.

values_and_stakes: Her academic scholarship and grades, which require her to manage stress and perform.
Her relationship with her parents, who would disapprove of her marijuana use and likely of counseling.
Her social standing and sense of belonging with her more sophisticated college peers.
key_facts: She uses marijuana a couple times a week, primarily to relax and try to fit in.
She bums marijuana from her roommate because she cannot afford it herself.
She has never talked to a counselor about her anxiety due to family stigma and perceived cost.

background: Chris is a high school or college student who is an honor student and a star athlete, living with parents who strictly monitor his social life.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as a recent, fun but risky deviation from his usual disciplined life, where drinking helped him socialize but led to betraying his mother's trust, losing focus on schoolwork, and changing friend groups.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes the severity of consequences when directly challenged, as seen in responding 'Kind of' when the therapist lists negative impacts.
Qualifies commitment to change with realistic exceptions, like allowing one drink at parties to fit in socially.
(inferred) Deflects from deeper self-examination by focusing on external factors (parental rules, friend invitations) rather than internal drivers.

ambivalence.for_change: He feels determined to change because he dislikes the guilt of betraying his mother and the physical unpleasantness of overdrinking.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to the social freedom and relaxation that drinking provides, seeing it as a way to escape his reserved, self-conscious identity.

values_and_stakes: Trust and approval from his mother, which he damaged by breaking his promise about alcohol.
His academic performance and status as an honor student, which is slipping due to lethargy and lack of focus.
His athletic standing and team role, which he implies is at risk if his performance declines.
key_facts: He lied to his mother about attending a party and drinking, and she detected vodka when picking him up.
He has started prioritizing partying and obtaining alcohol over studying, even before exams.
His social circle has shifted to friends associated with the party scene, creating tension with his old friends.

background: She is a parent with a 12-year-old daughter who is currently in the hospital; she works in an environment where smoking is a social activity with colleagues. (inferred)
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as a conflict between being a good parent and role model for her children, especially her 12-year-old daughter, and her personal enjoyment and reliance on smoking for stress relief, socializing, and weight control.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by emphasizing external life turmoil and lack of readiness when the therapist introduces the topic of quitting.
Lists multiple positive functions of smoking (social, stress relief, weight control) to justify maintaining the behavior when asked about change.
Responds with 'I can't think of anything' and states having no plans to quit when directly asked what would make quitting a higher priority.

ambivalence.for_change: She feels she is a bad role model for her children and is specifically worried her daughter will start smoking, which creates a pull toward quitting.
ambivalence.against_change: She is emotionally attached to smoking as a source of enjoyment, relaxation, social belonging, and weight control, and cannot imagine her life without it.

values_and_stakes: Her relationship with and role-modeling for her 12-year-old daughter.
Her social inclusion and bonding with coworkers during smoke breaks.
(inferred) Her sense of self-control over stress and weight management.
key_facts: Her daughter is currently in the hospital, which is the context for today's session.
She observed her daughter watching her smoke through a window this morning.
She agreed to schedule another appointment and to try a homework exercise about reasons for change.

background: A 20-year-old college student at Minnesota State Mankato, living away from parents who took his car after a DUI, and who faces potential suspension and being sent to work on his uncle's farm in Iowa.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as 'more of a getting caught problem' than a drinking problem, attributing his situation to bad luck compared to his friends who 'drink like fishes' and don't get caught.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by comparing himself favorably to peers ('normal college kid') and minimizing the drinking context ('not a big house party') when his behavior is discussed.
Shifts blame to external circumstances (the Vikings losing, inability to find a ride) when accounting for his decisions leading to the DUI.
(inferred) Resists internalizing the problem as his own by framing consequences (detox, parental punishment) as unfair or externally imposed hardships rather than results of his choices.

ambivalence.for_change: He admits that avoiding future problems with police and school is 'super important' because the detox experience was awful and he wants to succeed in college and become an international journalist.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to a social identity and lifestyle as a 'normal college kid' who drinks with friends, and changing that feels like a loss of belonging and fun.

values_and_stakes: His college education and the goal of becoming an international journalist, which requires good grades and avoiding suspension.
His social life and friendships at college, which he fears losing if sent to his uncle's farm in Iowa.
His relationship with his parents, whom he does not want to disappoint and who currently control his car and impose consequences.
key_facts: He was cited for driving under the influence at age 20 and transported to detox after drinking at a friend's house while watching a Vikings game.
His confidence in following through on a plan to drink less is a six out of ten.
He had a 3.5 GPA in high school and believes he could succeed academically in college if he reprioritized.

background: (inferred) A patient named David who is receiving dental care and has a history of smoking, with multiple health professionals (family doctor, cardiologist) also involved in his care.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as wanting to get his teeth fixed, not as needing to quit smoking, and sees previous quit attempts as causing more problems than they helped.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by minimizing the therapist's concern and redirecting to his immediate goal (e.g., 'I just want to get my teeth fixed')
Becomes defensive when feeling lectured or judged by authority figures (e.g., 'I get very defensive about when they bring-- cause I get it from my family doc, from my cardiologist')
Dismisses interventions by emphasizing past negative experiences (e.g., citing side effects and calling previous attempts 'a waste')

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He acknowledges smoking is harmful and that quitting is important for his health, as indicated by his past attempt and cooperation.
ambivalence.against_change: He feels quitting is not easy and that attempts cause more problems than they solve, creating a pull toward maintaining the status quo.

values_and_stakes: His immediate oral health goal (getting his teeth fixed) is at risk if the focus shifts to smoking cessation.
(inferred) His autonomy and self-image as 'not a complete fool' are at stake if he feels pressured or lectured.
(inferred) His comfort and avoidance of side effects from medications are at risk if he tries new interventions.
key_facts: He has tried medication to quit smoking before and experienced side effects.
Multiple health professionals (family doctor, cardiologist) have already advised him to quit smoking.
He explicitly states he does not want to discuss quitting smoking during this session.

background: Molly is a high school freshman (inferred) who is involved in swimming and has a close but sometimes strained relationship with her mother.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as being an 'easy target' for bullying because she 'nags on things' and can't leave confrontations alone, which makes rumors and drama worse.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by externalizing blame onto others (e.g., 'you're probably just jealous,' 'she's a nobody') when discussing social conflicts.
Minimizes her own emotional investment in past hurts by claiming she 'just forgot about it' after significant losses like a friendship.
Resists direct identification of specific peers who provoke her by withholding names ('there's like four main ones but not that like I can say who').

ambivalence.for_change: She wants to avoid getting in trouble and receiving her mother's silent treatment, which motivates her to walk away from provocations.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She feels a pull to defend herself and retaliate when provoked because not responding feels like allowing others to disrespect her.

values_and_stakes: Her relationship with her mother, which is strained when she gets in trouble.
Her small circle of trusted friends who provide support and validation.
(inferred) Her social standing and reputation at a large high school, where rumors can isolate her.
key_facts: She has stayed home from school twice due to bullying.
She successfully used a strategy of walking away once and felt proud.
She has a specific friend she considers bringing to therapy.

background: (inferred) A single woman who recently ended a six-year relationship about a year ago, now actively trying to meet new partners. Her social life revolves around going out with friends on weekends.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as her drinking having 'got a bit out of control' over the last six months, especially on weeknights, and it's not working to help her meet people while causing negative impacts like hangovers, poor eating, and lack of exercise.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes the severity of her drinking by comparing it to normative behavior ('like most people do').
Immediately qualifies a change goal with a statement protecting the behavior ('I don't wanna stop altogether').
(inferred) Attributes the problem to external circumstances (post-breakup, friends' habits) rather than internal drivers.

ambivalence.for_change: She feels a strong need to act because she sees the drinking is negatively impacting her health and routine, and she fears it will 'just get worse'.

values_and_stakes: Their identity as a 'good person' who helps people, which would be threatened by acting in a way they perceive as selfish or unkind.
The companionship and emotional security provided by having someone living with them.

key_facts: The client has already told the housemate to move out within a couple of days.
The housemate has other housing options available, which the client has discussed with them.

background: (inferred) A student living with her single mother, struggling financially and academically.
self_view_of_problem: She frames her problem as being 'stupid' and lacking willpower, seeing self-harm and suicide as the only way out of her pain and to relieve her mother's burden.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by insisting her self-destructive solution is correct when the therapist challenges it.
Shuts down with 'I don't know' and 'I'm not sure I can' when asked to consider alternative behaviors.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) She feels a pull toward change because she continues to attend therapy and school, and expresses a desire to help her mother.
ambivalence.against_change: She feels a pull away from change because she is emotionally attached to the belief that her death would solve her mother's problems.

values_and_stakes: Her relationship with and perceived burden on her single mother.
Her role as a 'good kid' who tries in school despite not having the best grades.
(inferred) Her own physical survival, which is at risk from self-harm and suicidal ideation.
key_facts: She engages in self-cutting to manage internal pain.
She has a C average in school with an A in math, her previously lowest subject.
She lives in a single-parent household where her mother pays for her food, uniforms, and shelter.

background: A pregnant woman referred by her doctor due to concerns about her alcohol intake during pregnancy. (inferred) She has a partner and socializes with friends.
self_view_of_problem: She does not see her alcohol intake as a problem; she frames it as a normal, culturally embedded practice (wine with supper as a family tradition) and views medical warnings as unsupported 'old wives' tales' that infringe on her autonomy.
resistance_drivers: Rejects external authority when it challenges her self-image as independent and autonomous (e.g., dismisses doctor's concerns and brochure as not being 'proof').
Uses selective evidence-seeking to confirm pre-existing beliefs (e.g., cites friends' experiences and online articles that support drinking during pregnancy).
Minimizes risk by normalizing her behavior (e.g., frames nightly wine as a harmless family tradition and questions the 'why' behind guidelines).

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) She feels a pull toward change because she deeply values having a healthy baby and being a good parent, which creates internal tension with her drinking.
ambivalence.against_change: She feels a strong emotional attachment to her autonomy and resistance to being controlled, viewing abstinence as an imposition on her independence and bodily autonomy.

values_and_stakes: Her identity as an independent person who makes her own choices ('I'm independent and I'm gonna do what I want, it's my body').
Her social and familial traditions around alcohol (wine at supper as a family tradition and a way to relax with friends).
Her relationship with her partner, who shares her view and whose support she seeks for any change.
key_facts: She drinks a glass of wine at supper every night and socially with friends.
She has personally known friends who drank during pregnancy without problems.
She requested to take the brochure home to show her partner and get their support.

background: He is a self-employed accountant who runs his own business, juggling a heavy workload that often requires him to work evenings and weekends.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as a lack of time due to his busy, self-employed lifestyle, stating 'food is just fuel' and that his weight is 'something I would like to get hold off' but is prevented by his schedule.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by citing external pressures (e.g., time, workload) when the therapist raises a topic he wants to avoid.
Expresses frustration and challenges the therapist's competence or respect (e.g., over being kept waiting) when feeling his time is not being valued.
Uses intellectualized agreement ('I'm aware of the problems, and I'm also aware of the solutions') to preemptively dismiss the need for discussion.

ambivalence.for_change: He admits he wants to lose weight, sees the link to his health (blood pressure, getting out of breath), and ideally would like things to be different.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to his identity as a busy, indispensable professional whose work justifies and excuses his current lifestyle.

values_and_stakes: His professional reputation and client relationships, which he believes depend on his constant availability and punctuality.
Control over his time and schedule, which he equates with being self-employed and successful.
(inferred) His self-concept as a competent, in-control person who 'juggles all these balls' and doesn't want to drop any.
key_facts: He was kept waiting for 45 minutes for this appointment and found it unacceptable.
He states that every moment out of his workday means he has to work evenings or weekends.
He agreed to a follow-up appointment only after the therapist proposed a specific 8:30 AM slot with no waiting.

background: He is a car salesman who is single and lives alone, with a social circle of friends from high school that he drinks with. He is attending a court-mandated assessment after his second DUI.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as 'poor judgment' and 'bad luck' rather than a drinking problem, stating 'it was an isolated incident' and 'I don't really think I have a problem with the drinking.'
resistance_drivers: Minimizes his drinking and its consequences when directly questioned about frequency or severity (e.g., 'I don't really remember,' 'it's not a habit').
Deflects responsibility by externalizing blame onto friends, luck, or his ex-girlfriend when his behavior is scrutinized.
Shifts to superficial compliance and practical solutions (like taxi money) when pressed about change, avoiding deeper self-examination.

ambivalence.for_change: He admits he doesn't want to lose his license or job and recognizes a need to avoid trouble, saying 'I don't wanna go through this again.'
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He fears losing his primary social identity and sense of belonging, as sobriety previously left him feeling isolated and bored without his friends.

values_and_stakes: His driver's license and job as a car salesman, which are concretely at risk if he gets another DUI.
His long-term friendships with his high school social circle, which are contingent on participating in drinking culture.
(inferred) His autonomy and self-image as an independent person not controlled by others, which he associates with his drinking lifestyle.
key_facts: He has received two DUIs, the most recent with a blood alcohol level of 2.8.
After his first DUI, he stopped drinking for six months, during which his friends withdrew and his relationship with his girlfriend became conflict-ridden before ending.
He plans to host a Super Bowl party at his house as a strategy to avoid driving after drinking.

background: He is training for a marathon and came to therapy for anxiety and insomnia. (inferred) He is likely a working-age male with a focus on health and fitness.
self_view_of_problem: He frames his problem as anxiety and insomnia that disrupt his marathon training, and he does not believe his drinking is a significant cause, stating 'I don't really think I drink that much in the first place' and that drinking helps him sleep.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes the severity of his drinking when confronted with data, e.g., 'I didn't think I was that bad' after being shown his drinking falls in a high-risk category.
Deflects by citing a perceived benefit of the behavior, e.g., arguing that on nights he doesn't drink he has a harder time going to sleep.
(inferred) Resists the 'alcoholic' label and identity threat, as shown by his need to distinguish himself from that category.

ambivalence.for_change: He wants to improve his sleep and health to succeed in his marathon training.
ambivalence.against_change: He is attached to drinking as a perceived sleep aid and to a self-image as a moderate, healthy person, not a 'hazardous drinker'.

values_and_stakes: His identity as a 'pretty healthy guy' and marathon trainee.
His perceived ability to manage sleep and anxiety without giving up a familiar coping mechanism.
(inferred) His social or weekend routines that involve drinking.
key_facts: He reported drinking two to three times a week, three to four drinks at a time, with weekly episodes of six or more drinks.
He wakes up around 2:00 AM on nights when he drinks too much.
When asked to set a goal, he proposed limiting himself to 18 drinks per week, which is still above the low-risk guideline of 14.
